L64: # Canine Osteosarcoma Trials
L65: 
L66: ## Clinical, Molecular, and Immune Characterization of Naturally Occurring Osteosarcoma in Dogs
L67: 
L68: ### Principal Investigator
L69: 
L70: Dr. Michael Childress, Professor of Comparative Oncology
L71: ### Background
L72: Osteosarcoma (OS) commonly occurs in the leg bones of large and giant breed dogs, such as Rottweilers, Saint Bernards, and Greyhounds. The standard treatment of OS involves surgical amputation of the affected leg followed by chemotherapy, which extends survival time for most dogs, while also preserving a good quality of life. However, up to 1/3 of dogs treated this way will die of cancer spread within 4-6 months, a time frame that is not much different from that of dogs treated by amputation only.
L73: To better understand the biological factors affecting this variability in survival time, we are enrolling dogs with OS in a study where they will be treated with amputation only . Dogs in this study may not receive chemotherapy or other tumor-targeting therapies after undergoing amputation. The dogs will be observed periodically at Purdue until the time of natural death or euthanasia due to OS.
L74: Tumor tissue samples, blood samples, and stool samples will be collected from these dogs at several time points to determine how the genetic makeup of the cancer, the immune system, and fecal microorganisms (i.e., “microbiome”) interact to affect the clinical aggressiveness of OS. This is a multi-institutional study currently being conducted at several US veterinary colleges.
L75: ### Eligibility for Dogs to Participate in the Study
L76:   * Histopathologically or cytologically confirmed OS of a long bone on the leg (humerus, radius, ulna, femur, tibia)
L77:     * Note that dogs can be enrolled based upon how the tumor appears on x-rays if previous attempts at biopsy or cytology were non-diagnostic
L78:   * Minimum body weight 25 kg (55 lbs.)
L79:   * Dogs must be able to walk well on 3 limbs, as determined by veterinarians at Purdue
L80:   * No evidence of cancer spread seen on baseline chest x-rays or abdominal sonogram
L81:   * Dogs must be generally healthy and capable to taking care of their basic needs (eating, drinking, urinating and defecating in appropriate places) at home
L82:   * Dogs must not have received prior treatment for osteosarcoma, including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, investigational therapies, or bisphosphonate drugs (e.g., zoledronate, pamidronate)
L83:   * Dogs can be enrolled in the trial if they have previously been treated with medications for pain, including NSAIDs (e.g. Rimadyl, Deramaxx, Previcox, Metacam)
L84: ### Exclusion Criteria
L85:   * Current use of medications that affect the function of the immune system
L86:     * Corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone, dexamethasone)
L87:     * Apoquel
L88:     * Cyclosporine
L89:     * Mycophenolate
L90:   * Significant comorbid disease that precludes safe anesthesia for surgery or may affect overall survival time
L91:     * Includes, but is not limited to, congestive heart failure, abnormal heart rhythms requiring medication, clinical bleeding disorders, liver failure, or kidney failure
L92:   * Hematocrit <25%
L93:   * Platelets <100,000/ul
L94:   * Clinically significant abnormalities on baseline blood tests (as determined by veterinarians at Purdue)
L95: ### Financial Support
L96: 
L97:   * The cost of baseline screening tests at Purdue to determine eligibility for the trial is capped at $100
L98:   * All costs related to the clinical trial are fully covered.
L99: 
L100: ### Trial Status
L101: 
L102:  Recruiting Paused at this Time
L103: 
L104: ### Questions
L105: 
L106: Call Dr. Michael Childress at 765-494-1107 or the Clinical Trial Nurses, Lindsey Fourez or Araynna Holland, at 765-494-1130 or 765-496-5966. Please leave a message for call back.

L109: ## Functional Imaging of Osteosarcoma to Improve Assessment of Immunotherapy Efficacy
L110: 
L111: ### Principal Investigator
L112: 
L113: Dr. Michael Childress, Professor of Comparative Oncology
L114: ### Background
L115: 
L116: Many of the dramatic recent successes in cancer therapy have come from drugs that activate the immune system to attack cancer. However, these drugs are typically very expensive and benefit only a relatively small fraction of all cancer patients. Advanced imaging tests provide detailed information about tumor biology, blood flow, and metabolism, some of which is related to the activity of the immune system within a tumor.
L117: We are currently studying osteosarcoma using two advanced imaging methods – dynamic contrast-enhanced computed tomography (DCE-CT) and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) – to better understand how treatments activate the immune system to attack this cancer. Dogs enrolled in this study will be placed under anesthesia to have DCE-CT and MRS performed on their primary tumor prior to undergoing surgical amputation.
L118: Samples will be collected from the tumor following amputation to examine the type of immune cells present within the tumor. Information learned from this study will serve as a baseline against which we can compare images from the tumors of dogs that have been treated with immune therapies.
L119: We ultimately plan to use this information to help us determine if an immune-targeting therapy is likely to activate the immune system and therefore benefit specific dogs, allowing us to personalize immune-targeted therapy in dogs with osteosarcoma.
L120: ### Eligibility for Dogs to Participate in the Study
L121:   * Histopathologically or cytologically confirmed osteosarcoma of a long bone on the leg (humerus, radius, ulna, femur, tibia)
L122:   * Dog owners must be willing to allow their dog to undergo surgical amputation of the affected leg
L123:   * Dogs must be considered healthy and fit enough to undergo general anesthesia and amputation, as determined by veterinarians at Purdue
L124:   * No evidence of cancer spread seen on baseline imaging tests done at Purdue (such as X-rays, ultrasound scans, or CT scans)
L125:   * Dogs must not have received prior treatment for osteosarcoma, including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, investigational therapies, or bisphosphonate drugs (e.g., zoledronate, pamidronate)
L126:   * Dogs can be enrolled in the trial if they have previously been treated with medications for pain, including NSAIDs (e.g. Rimadyl, Deramaxx, Previcox, Metacam)
L127: ### Exclusion Criteria
L128: 
L129:   * Current use of medications that affect the function of the immune system
L130:     * Corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone, dexamethasone)
L131:     * Apoquel
L132:     * Cyclosporine
L133:     * Mycophenolate
L134:   * Significant comorbid disease that precludes safe anesthesia and/or surgical amputation
L135:     * Includes, but is not limited to, congestive heart failure, abnormal heart rhythms requiring medication, clinical bleeding disorders, liver failure, or kidney failure
L136: ### Financial Support
L137: 
L138:   * All costs related to the study (imaging and anesthesia charges) are fully covered.
L139:   * A hospital credit in the amount of $2,000 is provided to the owners of all dogs participating in the study. This credit may be used to defray other expenses associated with osteosarcoma treatment, including cancer staging, surgery, and chemotherapy.
L140: 
L141: ### Trial Status
L142: 
L143: Actively Recruiting
L144: ### Questions
L145: 
L146: Call Dr. Michael Childress at 765-494-1107 or the Clinical Trial Nurses, Lindsey Fourez or Araynna Holland, at 765-494-1130 or 765-496-5966. Please leave a message for call back.

L150: ## Biodynamic Imaging to Predict Chemotherapy Response in Osteosarcoma
L151: 
L152: ### Principal Investigator
L153: 
L154: Dr. Michael Childress, Professor of Comparative Oncology
L155: ### Background
L156: Chemotherapy is part of the definitive treatment for dogs with osteosarcoma. It is typically given following surgical removal of the primary tumor and is intended to prevent or delay the growth of microscopic cancer that has spread (metastasized) to other organs, most often the lungs. By preventing the growth of microscopic cancer, chemotherapy extends survival for most dogs with osteosarcoma. The drugs carboplatin, cisplatin, and doxorubicin all improve survival times for dogs with osteosarcoma.
L157: However, some dogs benefit more from chemotherapy than others and the optimal chemotherapy drug for any individual dog's cancer is difficult to predict.
L158: We are currently studying a technique called biodynamic imaging (BDI) to determine whether it can predict the effectiveness of the drug carboplatin in individual dogs with osteosarcoma. Dogs enrolled in this study will undergo standard therapy consisting of a drug called carboplatin given once every 3 weeks for a total of 5 doses. After this, dogs will be screened with x-rays for cancer spread at Purdue every 3 months for up to 1 year.
L159: BDI data will be examined after the study is complete to determine the extent to which BDI predicts survival time.
L160: ### Eligibility for Dogs to Participate in the Study
L161:   * Histopathologically or cytologically confirmed osteosarcoma of a long bone on the leg (humerus, radius, ulna, femur, tibia).
L162:     * Cases in which imaging (CT, x-rays) findings are consistent osteosarcoma but attempts at biopsy have yielded non-diagnostic results may be entered on a case-by-case basis if osteosarcoma is highly suspected
L163:   * Dog owners must be willing to allow their dog to undergo surgical amputation of the affected leg
L164:   * Dog owners must be willing to bring their dogs back to Purdue for scheduled recheck examinations for up to 1 year following amputation surgery
L165:   * Dogs must be considered healthy and fit enough to undergo general anesthesia and amputation, as determined by veterinarians at Purdue
L166:   * No evidence of cancer spread seen on baseline imaging tests done at Purdue (such as X-rays, ultrasound scans, or CT scans)
L167:   * Dogs can be enrolled in the trial if they have previously been treated with medications for pain, including NSAIDs (e.g. Rimadyl, Deramaxx, Previcox, Metacam)
L168: ### Exclusion Criteria
L169: 
L170:   * Significant comorbid disease that precludes safe anesthesia and/or surgical amputation
L171:     * Includes, but is not limited to, congestive heart failure, abnormal heart rhythms requiring medication, clinical bleeding disorders, liver failure, or kidney failure)
L172:   * Dogs must not have received prior treatment for osteosarcoma, including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, investigational therapies, or bisphosphonate drugs (e.g., zoledronate pamidronate)
L173: ### Financial Support
L174: 
L175: A hospital credit in the amount of $1,000 is provided to the owners of all dogs participating in the study. This credit may be used to defray other expenses associated with osteosarcoma treatment, including cancer staging, surgery, and chemotherapy.
L176: 
L177: ### Trial Status
L178: 
L179: Actively Recruiting
L180: 
L181: ### Questions
L182: 
L183: Call Dr. Michael Childress at 765-494-1107 or the Clinical Trial Nurses, Lindsey Fourez or Araynna Holland, at 765-494-1130 or 765-496-5966. Please leave a message for call back.

L64: # Emerging Immunotherapy Study
L65: 
L66: ## SHP-1 Inhibitor (M029) Phase I Clinical Trial in Dogs with Cancer
L67: 
L68: ### Principal Investigators
L69: 
L70: Dr. Marejka Shaevitz and Dr. Debbie Knapp, Purdue University College of Veterinary Medicine
L71: ### Background
L72: 
L73: The immune system has a natural ability to recognize and attack cancer cells, but cancers can use several mechanisms to reduce this immune response. M029 is a new oral immunotherapy drug that blocks SHP-1, a protein that can limit immune system activity. By blocking SHP-1, researchers hope that M029 may allow the immune system to better recognize and attack cancer cells.
L74: M029 has been well tolerated in laboratory dogs, but this is the first clinical trial of M029 in pet dogs with naturally occurring cancer. The main goals of this Phase I study are to evaluate the safety of M029, learn how the drug moves through the body, determine whether it is having the expected effect on its target, and identify a dose that produces a biological effect. We will also look for any signs of anti-cancer activity in dogs receiving the drug.
L75: Because M029 is a new, first-in-class drug, there may be side effects that are not yet known. Possible side effects include stomach upset and effects from an overactive immune system, such as inflammation of organs or worsening of an underlying autoimmune disease. Dogs enrolled in the trial will be monitored closely for these and other possible side effects.
L76: M029 is given by mouth once daily. The dose will be gradually increased if the dog tolerates treatment well. Dogs will return to Purdue Veterinary Hospital Oncology every two weeks at first and then monthly for examinations, bloodwork, tumor measurements, and other monitoring. Some visits will last most of the day because several blood samples will be collected to measure drug levels and the drug's effects in the body.
L77: ### Eligibility for Dogs to Participate in the Study
L78: 
L79: Dogs may be eligible if they:
L80: 
L81:   * Are at least 1 year old and weigh at least 10 kg (22 pounds)
L82:   * Have a cancer diagnosis confirmed by cytology or biopsy
L83:   * Have a tumor that can be measured during a physical examination or on x-rays
L84:   * Have not yet received treatment for their cancer
L85:   * Are otherwise healthy and expected to live at least 18 weeks
L86:   * Can take oral medication at home on an empty stomach
L87: ### Exclusion Criteria
L88: 
L89: Dogs may not be eligible if they have:
L90: 
L91:   * A history or evidence of autoimmune disease
L92:   * Certain endocrine, heart, or other significant diseases
L93:   * Received chemotherapy or radiation therapy within the previous 3 months
L94:   * Previously received immunotherapy
L95:   * Recently received steroids, NSAIDs, herbal products, CBD, or other supplements
L96: 
L97: Final eligibility will be determined by the study team after review of the dog's medical history and screening results.
L98: ### Financial Support
L99: 
L100: M029 is provided at no cost to owners. Owners are responsible for the costs of initial cancer diagnosis and staging before enrollment. Once enrolled, owners pay a flat fee of $350 per month to help cover bloodwork and study monitoring.
L101: 
L102: If an emergency visit is required because of a suspected treatment-related side effect, the study may provide up to $500 toward the cost of that visit. The study will also cover the cost of a necropsy if a participating dog dies or is euthanized.
L103: ### Trial Status
L104: 
L105: Actively Recruiting
L106: 
L107: ### Questions
L108: 
L109: For more information about the SHP-1 clinical trial or to find out whether your dog may be eligible, please contact Dr. Marejka Shaevitz or the Clinical Trial Technician Holly Aschliman by calling 765-494-1107 or emailing SHP1Canine@purdue.edu.
